bites.title: Strings, numbers, and booleans
bites.body: Python values have types. Text in quotes is a string, like "hello". Whole numbers and decimals are numbers, like 2 and 2.5. A boolean is only True or False, with those capitals. The quoted word "True" is text, not a boolean. When you read AI-written code, name the type of each value before you trust how it is used.
bites.sourceNote: Python language reference, built-in types · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which of these is a boolean?
questions.explanation: True and False, with capitals and no quotes, are booleans. "True" is a string. 1 is a number, even though Python treats True as equal to 1.
2.5 is a float, one of Python's number types. A string would be in quotes.

bites.title: Lists, dictionaries, sets, and tuples
bites.body: A list keeps items in order, and you can change it: ["red", "blue"]. A tuple is also ordered, but it is fixed, like ("red", "blue"). A dictionary maps a key to a value and keeps keys in the order you added them: {"name": "Eric"}. A set holds unique items and does not promise an order. Duplicates in a set disappear.
bites.sourceNote: Python tutorial, data structures · confidence: high

questions.prompt: You need a name-to-score mapping you can look up by name. What fits?
questions.explanation: A dictionary stores a value under a key, so a name can point at a score.

questions.prompt: What happens when you add the same item to a set twice?

choices.text: It is stored twice, in order
Python turns it into a list

questions.explanation: A set drops duplicates. It also does not give you an order you can rely on.

bites.title: Mutability
bites.body: Some values can be changed in place. Lists, dictionaries, and sets can. Strings and tuples cannot: any "change" builds a new value. If two names point at the same list, editing it through one name shows up on the other. That surprise is common in generated code. A second name is not a copy. Use .copy() when you need a separate list.
bites.sourceNote: Python data model, mutable vs immutable objects · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Two variables name the same list. You append an item through the first. What does the second see?

choices.text: The list with the new item

questions.explanation: Both names refer to one list object. Appending changes that object, so both names see it.

questions.prompt: Which value cannot be changed in place?
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable. Methods like replace return a new string rather than editing the old one.

bites.title: Strings, numbers, booleans
bites.body:
Every value in Python has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it. Think of containers in a kitchen: a jug holds liquid, a tin holds biscuits, and you would not pour soup into the biscuit tin.

A string is text in quotes, like "hello". Numbers come as whole numbers (2) or decimals (2.5). A boolean is only True or False, with a capital letter and no quotes.

The catch: "True" in quotes is text, not a boolean. When you read AI-written code, name the type of each value before you trust how it is used.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which of these is a boolean?
questions.explanation: True and False, capitalised and without quotes, are the booleans. "True" in quotes is a string that only looks like one.

bites.title: Lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples
bites.body:
These are Python's four everyday ways to hold many values.

A list is a numbered queue: ["red", "blue"]. Order matters and you can change it. A tuple is a list that is sealed after it is made: ("red", "blue"). A dictionary is a labelled filing cabinet: {"name": "Eric"}, where you look things up by key. A set is a bag of unique items: add "red" twice and it holds one.

Choosing between them is a real decision. Code that uses a list to check "have I seen this before?" works, but gets slow as it grows. A set answers that question instantly.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: You need to look up a person's score by their name. Which structure fits best?
questions.explanation: A dictionary stores a value under a key, so the name can point straight at the score.

bites.title: Mutability (concept)
bites.body:
Mutable means "can be changed in place". Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable. Strings and tuples are not: any "change" quietly builds a new value.

Here is why it matters. Picture a shared online document. If you send a friend the link, you both edit the same document. In Python, b = a on a list hands over the link, not a photocopy. Change b and a changes too.

This is a classic surprise in generated code. When you truly need a separate copy, the code should say so with a.copy().
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: a is a list and you write b = a, then add an item to b. What happens to a?

choices.text: Nothing, because b is an independent copy
It gains the item too, because both names point at the same list

questions.explanation: Assignment gives a second name to the same list. Only an explicit copy, such as a.copy(), makes a separate one.

bites.title: Lists hold ordered items; dictionaries hold labelled data
bites.body:
Most data you meet in AI work is built from just these two shapes.

Use a list when the items are the same kind of thing and order matters: the messages in a chat, the rows in a file, the steps in a plan. You reach an item by its position, counting from 0.

Use a dictionary when each piece has a name: {"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}. You reach a value by its label, not its position.

They nest. A chat history is a list of dictionaries: an ordered run of messages, each with labelled parts. Spotting that shape makes API code far easier to read.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: A chat history sent to an LLM is usually shaped as:

choices.text: A list of dictionaries, one per message
A dictionary of tuples keyed by time

questions.explanation: The messages are ordered (a list) and each one has labelled parts such as role and content (a dictionary).

bites.title: JSON maps directly onto dictionaries and lists
bites.body:
JSON is the text format most APIs speak. The good news: it has almost the same shapes as Python. A JSON object {} becomes a dictionary. A JSON array [] becomes a list. Strings and numbers carry straight over.

So when an API replies with {"items": [{"id": 1}]}, Python sees a dictionary holding a list of dictionaries, and data["items"][0]["id"] walks down to the 1.

Small differences to remember: JSON writes true, false and null in lowercase, and Python turns them into True, False and None. JSON also insists on double quotes.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: A JSON array, once loaded into Python, becomes a:
questions.explanation: JSON arrays map to Python lists, and JSON objects map to dictionaries.

bites.title: None: the value that means "nothing here"
bites.body:
None is Python's way to say "there is no value". It is not zero, not an empty string and not False. Think of a form: a box where someone wrote 0 is different from a box left blank. None is the blank box.

You will see it constantly. A function with no return gives back None. A lookup that finds nothing often returns None.

The classic crash is using None as if it were real data, such as asking for result["name"] when result is None. Careful code checks first: if result is None. Generated code often skips that check.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: A Python function has no return statement. What does calling it give back?
questions.explanation: A function that ends without returning anything hands back None automatically.

bites.title: Why types matter: "5" is text, 5 is a number
bites.body:
"5" and 5 look alike to a person, but Python treats them as different things. "5" + "5" glues text together and gives "55". 5 + 5 does arithmetic and gives 10. Mix them, "5" + 5, and Python stops with an error rather than guess.

This matters because nearly everything arriving from outside starts life as text: what a user types, a spreadsheet cell, a web form. The code must convert it, int("5"), before doing maths.

When totals in generated code look wildly wrong, check whether numbers are secretly strings.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.explanation: Both values are strings, so + joins them end to end instead of adding.
